messages.subject: Re: replicate lines and one-sided lines
messages.body_plain:
Laurent:

I'm sure several people on this list will want to tell you about the
'challenges' you face by detecting animals from a vehicle.  It seems
unlikely that you can drive the vehicle randomly through the vineyard
(at least you cannot do this with the vineyard owner's permission).
Without that random component, you face the issue that the hares you
wish to study are not distributed  in the vineyard at uniform distances
from where you are driving (tracks of some sort).  This will cause you
many problems with regard to the interpretation of the distribution of
detection distances.  This was most recently discussed on this list in a
message fro 6 November by Len Thomas (consult the Distance list archives
to find this message).  In that message, Len sends interested readers to
an advanced treatment of this topic within a dissertation by Tiago
Marques found at

http://hdl.handle.net/10023/391

If/when you resolve those issues, you will then be able to address the question of specifying a multiplier for
one-sided transects (found in Chapter 8 of the Users Guide, under the heading 'Multipliers in CDS analysis').
And regarding repeat visits over a transect, you can multiply the length of the transect by the number of
times it is travelled and use that as the amount of effort associated with that transect.

Laurent TATIN Laurent Tatin Mas petit Rebattu Moules F-13280

messages.subject: Re: replicate lines and one-sided lines
messages.body_plain:
Hi Laurent, list,

I add to Eric's message that 1 sided transects are usually discouraged,
being potentially problematic unless there is a very clear definition of
what is the transect line. Otherwise there is a tendency to record
animals "just on the other side" that the driver (using your wording)
records as "on the line". This leads to too many detections at 0 and a
corresponding overestimation of density. But as Eric said, this will
only be an issue to worry about once you have dealt with the non-uniform
distribution of distances which you seem to have to deal with at present.

It was not clear from your description if the lines are placed along
roads, or trails, or any other linear feature that the hares might
respond to. Feel free to contact me off the line if you want to explain
this further.

All the best,

Tiago

Laurent TATIN Laurent Tatin Mas petit Rebattu Moules F-13280=20

messages.subject: Re: pooling or not pooling f(0)
messages.body_plain:
I clarified off-list that there are just 2 observers - one on each side
of the plane.

One further question.  Do you also have different spatial strata that
are not equally sampled?  If you do not, then I think you are making
this too difficult.
All you need to do is setup year as the stratification variable and look
at MCDS models say ~1 (NULL), ~Observer, ~Year ~Observer+Year and
~Observer*Year.  Then compute
an estimate of abundance/density for each year with the global detection
function option.  Presumably you want a separate estimate for each
year.  The only difficulty will be that unless the model is
~Year or ~Observer*Year then your yearly estimates have a covariance due
to the commonality of the detection function model.  The model ~Observer
is pooled over years.  The model ~Observer+Year has an additive effect
of year and observer.  The model ~Observer*Year would be equivalent to
fitting the ~Observer model for each year separately.  If you fit
~Observer*Year and estimate abundance for each year and then select each
year and fit ~Observer, then the results for each year should be the
same and the sum of the AICs for the detection functions for each year
should match the AIC from the pooled analysis with ~Observer*Year as
long as you use the same key function and have no adjustment functions.

--jeff

messages.subject: Re: pooling or not pooling f(0)
messages.body_plain:
I clarified off-list that there are just 2 observers - one on each side
of the plane.

One further question.  Do you also have different spatial strata that
are not equally sampled?  If you do not, then I think you are making
this too difficult.
All you need to do is setup year as the stratification variable and look
at MCDS models say ~1 (NULL), ~Observer, ~Year ~Observer+Year and
~Observer*Year.  Then compute
an estimate of abundance/density for each year with the global detection
function option.  Presumably you want a separate estimate for each
year.  The only difficulty will be that unless the model is
~Year or ~Observer*Year then your yearly estimates have a covariance due
to the commonality of the detection function model.  The model ~Observer
is pooled over years.  The model ~Observer+Year has an additive effect
of year and observer.  The model ~Observer*Year would be equivalent to
fitting the ~Observer model for each year separately.  If you fit
~Observer*Year and estimate abundance for each year and then select each
year and fit ~Observer, then the results for each year should be the
same and the sum of the AICs for the detection functions for each year
should match the AIC from the pooled analysis with ~Observer*Year as
long as you use the same key function and have no adjustment functions.

--jeff

Magaly Chambellant wrote:
> > Good Day,
> >
> > I have been "playing" with my data and Distance for while, trying to improve
> > my analyses as I learn more from the book and the material from the
> > workshop. But I came across a problem that I cannot figure out.
> >
> > Here a summary of what I did (I will try to be concise):
> >
> > aerial survey, systematic line-transect
> > 2 independent observers on each side of the plane
> > 2 years of data
> >
> > Question of interest: density and abundance for each year
> >
> > I ran MCDS and tested 4 covariates of which only observer had an effect on
> > the detection function. So I post-stratified by observer and since I wanted to
> > have estimates for each year separately, I used the "data selection" to look at
> > each year individually. So I ran 2 analysis (1 for each year). For each analysis,
> > D and N were computed for each observer and for both observer pooled (mean
> > weighted by total effort in the stratum).
> >
> > But then, I realised that since the detection function was the same between
> > years for each observer, it would probably be better to estimate a pooled f(0)
> > over the 2 years for each observer and used the pooled f(0) to compute the
> > density and abundance estimates for each year and each observer.
> > The only way I managed to do this was to post-stratify by year and then
> > select for each observer. So I ran 2 analysis (1 for each observer). For each
> > analysis, D and N were computed for each year but with a pooled f(0) over
> > the 2 years. Then, to obtain overall (both observers combined) estimates of D
> > and N for each year, I ran an analysis with year as a stratum and with no data
> > selection.
> >
> > My thoughs were this latter option was a better approach but I am a bit
> > concerned because the estimates are different and, more importantly, have a
> > higher CV than with the first method. I am not totally sure I understand why is
> > that. For what I understood, in the first option the pooled estimates are
> > weighted means whereas the second option computed estimates from the
> > data of both observers combined, so that would explain why the values are
> > different and I would tend to think that the second option is better. But I still
> > don't understand why the CV would be increased (8.51 vs. 6.87 and 10.41 vs.

messages.body_plain:
Hello,

My question pertains to the validity of using DISTANCE sampling to estima=
te=20
detection probabilities and densities for bird data collected using BBS s=
tyle=20
road point transects and on trails in the grasslands ecozone of Canada.=20=

The purpose of this study was to determine differences in grassland bird=20=

density between roadside point transects and off-road point transects wit=
h=20
the ultimate goal of modeling species' distrbutions across the landscape=20=

(however, estimating detection probabilities is the first major hurdle).

Combined auditory and visual fixed-radius point counts were conducted alo=
ng=20
roads (secondary and dirt) and trail routes (no defined road and no ditch=
es)=20
with point count stations every 800m. Point transects on roads were=20
conducted along a 32km stretch for a total of 40 point count stations on =
a=20
route. Walking routes were paired with the road routes and generally star=
ted=20
at the sixth stop of the road route. The first stop of the walking route =
was at=20
least 800 m from the road and ran perpendicular to the road for 5 stops,=20=

paralleled the road for 2 stops, and returned towards the road for anothe=
r 4=20
stops. Bird detections were binned in the field into 100-m and 400-m band=
s=20
and each point count was 3-minutes in length (with no time intervals).

The ditches along the roads are ~20m wide (+12m wide road) and generally=20=

consist of taller non-native vegetation than the native prairie habitat t=
hrough=20
which the trail point transects were placed. Therefore, one can imagine t=
he=20
potentially large influence of the road and ditch on bird behaviour (avoi=
dance=20
or attraction) and bird species composition.=20

I understand the assumptions that are violated when roadside sampling is=20=

used; however, I am looking for a way in which to get around this problem=
. My=20
questions are as such:

1) Is it possible to estimate detection probability of birds using DISTAN=
CE for=20
data collected with only 2 distance bands (e.g., using the half-normal bi=
nomial=20
estimator)?

2) Can detection probablities for birds detected on roads be estimated by=
=20
combining all the trail and a random sample of the road point transect da=
ta=20
and (with survey type- trail or road as a covariate) then use detection=20=

probability estimates for each survey type to transform the estimates for=
 the=20
respective survey types?

Thank you in advance for any comments or suggestions!

Kevin Kardynal, MSc

messages.subject: Re: specifying multiplier with web data
messages.body_plain:
John F Lehmkuhl wrote:
> > I have trapping web data for small mammals over 4 nights.  I entered the
> > data as I would for point transects with Visits=4 and the multiplier as
> > "/".  However, wouldn't Visits=1 with trapping web data because I am using
> > 1st captures only (at this point in the analysis)?
> >

Correct.  With the point transect example, these would be 4 independent
samples of the same point. In the
trapping web example, you are removing seen animals at each occasion.
These are then "summed" for the
equivalent of a single visit.
